title: Grade 7 Science — Fri, May 22
description: Nutrition in Animals — Day 5 of 5: Complex reasoning (Synthesis)
subject: science

questions.question: A person's gall bladder is surgically removed. Which digestion process would be MOST affected?
options: Fat digestion — bile cannot be stored and released in concentrated doses
questions.explanation: Without a gall bladder, bile still flows from liver but continuously (not in concentrated doses). Fat emulsification is less efficient, making fat digestion harder.

questions.question: If a person had NO stomach acid (HCl), what would most likely happen?
options: Proteins would not be properly digested (pepsin needs acid), and bacteria would survive — causing infection
questions.explanation: HCl activates pepsin for protein digestion AND kills ingested bacteria. Without it: protein digestion fails in stomach AND food-borne pathogens survive.

questions.question: Why must glucose pass through the liver before reaching the brain or muscles?
options: The liver regulates blood glucose levels — storing excess as glycogen or releasing more when needed
Glucose is only made in the liver
questions.explanation: The hepatic portal vein carries absorbed glucose to the liver. The liver acts as a blood glucose regulator: storing excess (as glycogen) or releasing more — maintaining stable blood sugar.

questions.question: Amoeba digests food in a 'food vacuole'. This is similar to which part of human digestion?
options: The stomach — an enclosed compartment with digestive enzymes
questions.explanation: Both the food vacuole (in amoeba) and the stomach (in humans) are enclosed spaces where enzymes digest food. The food vacuole is amoeba's 'stomach'.

questions.question: After a large meal, blood glucose rises. Insulin is released by the pancreas. What does insulin do?
options: Breaks down fats in the intestine
Signals liver and muscle cells to take up glucose and store it as glycogen — lowering blood sugar
questions.explanation: Insulin is the hormone that lowers blood glucose after a meal. It signals cells to absorb glucose for energy or storage (glycogen in liver/muscles).

questions.question: A child eats a meal of dal-rice. Trace the journey of protein from dal, from ingestion to use by a muscle cell:
options: Protein → stomach (pepsin) → peptides → small intestine (proteases) → amino acids → blood → liver → muscle cells → new muscle protein
questions.explanation: Protein digestion: mouth (no change) → stomach (pepsin, HCl → peptides) → small intestine (trypsin, peptidases → amino acids) → blood capillaries → liver → bloodstream → muscle cells → used to make muscle proteins.

questions.question: If the small intestine of a person had NO villi, how would nutrition be affected?
options: Nutrient absorption would be severely reduced (dramatically less surface area) — person would be malnourished even eating well
The large intestine would compensate completely
questions.explanation: Villi increase surface area by ~10 times. Without villi, absorption is drastically reduced. The person would absorb only a fraction of available nutrients, leading to malnutrition.

questions.question: Roughage (fibre) is not digested, yet doctors say it is essential. The best explanation is:
options: It provides bulk that stimulates peristalsis, preventing constipation, and feeds beneficial gut bacteria
It digests slowly and provides extra proteins
It dissolves in blood and prevents heart disease directly
questions.explanation: Fibre has two important roles: mechanical (adds bulk → stimulates gut movement → prevents constipation) and microbial (feeds beneficial bacteria that produce vitamins and strengthen immunity).

questions.question: Why do newborn babies get their initial immunity from breast milk?
options: Breast milk contains the mother's antibodies (especially in colostrum) that protect the baby until its own immune system matures
Babies make their own antibodies from birth
questions.explanation: Colostrum (first milk) is rich in IgA antibodies. These are absorbed by the baby's immature gut and provide passive immunity against common pathogens.

questions.question: A patient cannot digest fats well after the pancreas is damaged. This is because:
options: The pancreas produces lipase — the main fat-digesting enzyme — which cannot reach the small intestine properly
questions.explanation: Pancreatic lipase is essential for fat digestion. Pancreatic damage reduces lipase output, so fats pass through undigested — causing fatty stools (steatorrhoea).

questions.question: Herbivores that eat only cellulose-rich grass can sustain themselves because:
options: Grass has more protein than meat
They evolved with gut bacteria (like Clostridium) that produce cellulase — breaking down cellulose that the animal cannot
Grass is easily digested by all animals
questions.explanation: Mammals cannot produce cellulase. Ruminants host cellulose-fermenting bacteria in their rumen or cecum — the microbiome effectively extends the animal's digestive capacity.

questions.question: Why is the pH DIFFERENT in the mouth (neutral, pH 7), stomach (acidic, pH 2), and small intestine (alkaline, pH 8)?
options: Different enzymes work at different pH; each section has the right pH for its specific enzymes (amylase: neutral; pepsin: acid; trypsin: alkaline)
All enzymes work at the same pH
questions.explanation: Each enzyme has an optimal pH for its specific shape. The different sections are specifically tailored to create optimal conditions for the enzymes that work there.

questions.question: After drinking a large amount of salty water, the body: (a) becomes dehydrated, (b) drinks more water, (c) excretes excess salt in urine. Which best explains why salty food makes us thirsty?
options: High salt concentration in blood draws water out of body cells by osmosis — cells signal thirst to restore water balance
questions.explanation: High blood salt (sodium) creates an osmotic gradient — water leaves cells to dilute blood. Cells shrink slightly, which brain detects as thirst. Drinking water restores balance.

questions.question: A doctor advises a patient to eat more probiotic foods (yoghurt, fermented foods). Why?
options: Probiotics introduce beneficial bacteria to the gut — improving digestion, immune function, and preventing harmful bacteria from thriving
Fermented food digests itself so the stomach works less
questions.explanation: The gut microbiome (trillions of gut bacteria) aids digestion, produces vitamins (K, B12), competes with pathogens, and trains the immune system. Probiotics maintain this healthy microbial community.

questions.question: The human digestive system is often compared to an 'assembly line in reverse'. Why is this apt?
options: Food assembles into bigger molecules as it passes through
Large, complex molecules are progressively broken down (disassembled) at each stage into simple, absorbable units — like a factory dismantling a product
The mouth is the output end
questions.explanation: An assembly line builds complex things from parts. The digestive system does the opposite — it systematically dismantles complex molecules (proteins, starch, fats) into their simplest building blocks (amino acids, glucose, fatty acids).
